discovery: Development of high-resolution angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) into a momentum-resolved probe of quantum materials, revealing the d-wave gap and pseudogap of high-temperature superconductors

nominees.name: Zhi-Xun Shen
nominees.affiliation: Stanford University and SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory, USA

nominees.name: Juan Carlos Campuzano
nominees.affiliation: University of Illinois Chicago and Argonne National Laboratory, USA

subfield: Condensed matter physics (experimental spectroscopy of correlated electrons)
motivation: Shen and Campuzano turned photoemission from a coarse band-mapping tool into a precise, momentum-resolved measurement of the single-particle spectral function in strongly correlated matter. Pushing energy and momentum resolution, they gave the first direct observation of the anisotropic, d-wave superconducting gap in the cuprates (Shen, 1993) and discovered the normal-state pseudogap and its Fermi-arc structure (Shen; Campuzano, Norman and co-workers, 1996-98). They also found the kinks that reveal electron-boson coupling. These results settled long-running debates about pairing symmetry and defined the central puzzles of cuprate physics. Their methods, now used at synchrotrons and laboratories worldwide, underpin the discovery and characterization of topological insulators, Weyl semimetals, iron-based superconductors and moire systems. Few experimental techniques have changed how we see electrons in solids so completely. This is a new way of seeing matter that has answered fundamental questions for three decades.
